title: The lab calls with a potassium
objective: Recognize high potassium -- above 5.1 mEq/L -- by cramping, diarrhea and peaked T waves, and report it as a risk for dysrhythmia

sources.note: Relayed from the REQ-233 NCLEX-PN cases (read 2026-11-11, primary PDF), not re-read: Coordinated Care includes care within the legal scope of practice; Physiological Adaptation includes recognizing and reporting a change in the client's condition.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

sources.cite: OpenStax, Fundamentals of Nursing (2024), section 20.1 (Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
sources.note: Relayed from the NCLEX course seed (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/nursing.ts, accessed 2026-11-02), not re-read: serum potassium above 5.1 mEq/L is hyperkalemia, recognized by irritability, cramping, diarrhea and peaked T waves, and it can progress to dysrhythmia and cardiac arrest; causes include kidney failure, potassium-sparing diuretics and supplements.

sources.cite: UK Kidney Association. Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Hyperkalaemia in Adults (updated July 2026)
sources.note: Relayed from the NCLEX-RN case hyperkalemia-critical-value (read 2026-11-14 in the primary PDF through a summarizing fetch with quotes), not re-read: severe hyperkalemia is 6.5 mmol/L or more (equal to mEq/L), with at least continuous ECG monitoring; peaked T waves, flattened P waves and a wide QRS, then bradycardia, sine wave and VT. A UK guideline; the facility's transfer policy follows it on monitoring.

brief.situation: 06:40 in a skilled nursing facility. You are the LPN on the rehab hall. The lab phones a critical result for Mr. Whitfield, 78: potassium 6.9 mEq/L on this morning's draw.
handover: Heart failure and chronic kidney disease. Medicines include lisinopril, spironolactone and a potassium chloride tablet, due at 08:00.
Overnight the aide noted three loose stools; he said his legs felt 'heavy and crampy'.

Facility policy: a critical lab value is read back and reported to the RN supervisor and the provider at once; any licensed nurse may call 911 for a resident with a critical value and symptoms; the LPN takes vital signs and an apical pulse and may hold a scheduled dose pending the provider's call.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the result means for him, what to hold and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What does a potassium of 6.9 mean for Mr. Whitfield, and what do you do as the LPN?

parts.label: What it means
parts.criteria: Potassium well above 5.1 (severe at 6.5 or more), with cramps, weakness, diarrhea and an irregular slow pulse, on spironolactone, lisinopril and a supplement with kidney disease: a risk of dysrhythmia and arrest.
parts.modelAnswer: Normal is up to 5.1; 6.9 is severe. His cramps, weakness, diarrhea and an irregular slow pulse fit, and his spironolactone, lisinopril, potassium tablet and kidney disease explain it. It can cause a dangerous rhythm.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Reads the result back; checks vital signs and an apical pulse; holds the potassium chloride; reports to the RN and provider at once (not after a redraw); 911 per policy; leaves IV treatment and ECG interpretation to the RN and hospital.
parts.modelAnswer: Read it back, check his vital signs and apical pulse, hold the potassium tablet, and report to the RN supervisor and provider now with SBAR. With symptoms, 911 per policy. Treatment like IV calcium is for the hospital team.

noProgress.rationale: A critical potassium with symptoms unreported an hour on is harm here.

scoring.modelReasoning: Potassium above 5.1 mEq/L is high and 6.9 is severe; his cramps, weakness, diarrhea and an irregular slow pulse fit, and spironolactone, lisinopril, a potassium supplement and kidney disease explain it. It can progress to dysrhythmia and arrest. Within the PN's scope: read the result back, check vital signs and an apical pulse, hold the potassium chloride pending the provider, and report to the RN supervisor and provider at once, with 911 per facility policy for a symptomatic critical value. Treatment is for the hospital team.
